reading.reading_name: Guidance for Standard IV: Duties to Employers

drills.los_text: demonstrate a thorough knowledge of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct by interpreting the Code and Standards in various situations involving issues of professional integrity
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard IV: Duties to Employers

questions.stem: Magee manages pension accounts at Trust Assets. Before resigning to join Fiduciary Management, he asks four of his largest accounts to leave Trust Assets and open accounts with Fiduciary, and he persuades prospects he had earlier presented to on behalf of Trust Assets to sign with Fiduciary instead. His conduct is most likely:

options.A: a violation as to both the clients and the prospects.
options.B: a violation as to the prospects only.
options.C: not a violation.

rationales.A: Magee's duty is to Trust Assets as long as he is employed there, and the employer-employee principle requires him to act solely for his employer's benefit. His solicitation of Trust Assets' current clients and of its prospective clients while still employed by the firm is unethical and violates Standard IV(A). Both groups are covered: the prospects were developed through presentations made on the firm's behalf, and the four large accounts are the firm's clients, not his.
rationales.B: Soliciting current clients and prospective clients while still employed both violate Standard IV(A), so the breach is not limited to the prospects. Informing existing clients of a move is not unconditionally permitted while the duty of loyalty is still owed; a departing employee may tell clients of the change only after leaving, and may not solicit them before.
rationales.C: This conflates permissible preparation to compete, which a departing employee may undertake on his own time, with the prohibited solicitation of the employer's clients and prospects while still employed. Preparation is allowed; diverting the employer's business before resigning is not.

questions.stem: Hightower has spent 15 years at Jason Investment and is planning to leave to start his own investment management business. Before resigning he intends to copy the firm's client list, account statements, marketing presentations and recommended list, the computer models for asset allocation and stock selection, and his own spreadsheets. Without Jason Investment's consent, Hightower is most likely permitted to copy:

options.A: none of the materials.
options.B: the lists and models he developed or maintained.
options.C: all of the materials, if used only after he resigns.

rationales.A: Except with the consent of their employer, departing members and candidates may not take employer property, which includes books, records, reports and other materials, because taking such materials may interfere with the employer's business opportunities. Taking any employer records, even those the member or candidate prepared, violates Standard IV(A). Employer records include items stored in hard copy or in any other medium, such as home computers, portable storage devices and cell phones.
rationales.B: Books, records, reports and similar materials created for the employer are the employer's property regardless of who built them. Fifteen years of developing and maintaining the client list and the allocation and selection models gives Hightower no right to copy them; records the member or candidate personally prepared are expressly covered.
rationales.C: Taking employer property without consent is itself the violation, so the timing of later use does not cure it. Waiting until the resignation becomes effective does not convert firm records into his own.

questions.stem: Madeline, a CFA candidate, spends a summer as an unpaid intern at Murdoch, where she helps develop GIPS-compliance software using firm resources. On leaving to join McMillan, she copies the software because she believes it will help her in the new job. Her copying of the software is most likely:

options.A: permitted, as candidates are not bound by the Standards.
options.B: a violation, as she is treated as a Murdoch employee.
options.C: permitted, as an unpaid intern owes no employee duties.

rationales.A: Candidates in the CFA Program are fully bound by the Code and Standards, so candidate status is no shelter. Madeline's conduct is judged exactly as a member's would be.
rationales.B: Even though Madeline receives no monetary compensation for her services at Murdoch, she used firm resources in creating the software and is considered an employee because she receives compensation and benefits in the form of work experience and knowledge. By copying the software, Madeline violated Standard IV(A) because she misappropriated Murdoch's property without permission.
rationales.C: An unpaid intern who uses firm resources is treated as an employee for purposes of Standard IV(A), because the work experience and knowledge gained are themselves compensation. The software she helped build with those resources is Murdoch's property, and copying it without permission is misappropriation.

questions.stem: Nash resigns after unsuccessful attempts to change his firm's churning practices and sends clients a farewell notice that the firm authorized. When one client asks about the circumstances of his departure, he describes the unethical practices in detail, gives her information about his new employer, and encourages her to follow him. Nash's conduct most likely:

options.A: violated the Standards by disparaging and soliciting.
options.B: violated the Standards only through the farewell notice.
options.C: complied, given the firm's churning practices.

rationales.A: Nash violated Standard IV(A) by disparaging his current employer to his client and soliciting her business for his future employer. His actions are a violation even if the client would be better off at the new firm. After leaving the firm, Nash can inform his former clients of his concerns about their treatment and suggest that they change investment managers; the fault is in doing so while still employed.
rationales.B: The farewell notice was authorized by the firm and was itself proper, so it is not the source of the breach. The violation lies in the disparagement of the employer and the solicitation of the client's business that followed her question.
rationales.C: A client-protection motive does not authorize disparaging the current employer and soliciting business for a future one while still employed. The conduct is a violation even if the client would in fact be better off at the new firm; the proper course is to raise the concerns after leaving.

questions.stem: Elliot has hired Chisolm away from a competing firm, and Chisolm, who knows her former clients well, now wants to contact them. No agreement between Chisolm and her former employer restricts such contact. Most likely, Chisolm:

options.A: may rebuild her former client list from memory.
options.B: may not contact them using records taken from the firm.
options.C: may never contact a client she served at the former firm.

rationales.A: Simple knowledge of the names and existence of former clients is not confidential information, but reconstructing the former employer's client list, from memory or otherwise, is still the use of information belonging to that firm. The records themselves are the firm's property, and recreating them does not change their ownership.
rationales.B: Because client records are the property of the firm, contacting former clients for any reason through the use of client lists or other information taken from a former employer without permission is a violation of Standard IV(A). Simple knowledge of the names and existence of former clients is not confidential information, and skills or experience obtained while employed are not confidential or privileged information. In the absence of an agreement prohibiting such conduct, as long as Chisolm maintains her duty of loyalty before joining Elliot's firm, takes no steps to solicit clients until she has left the former firm, and does not use material from her former employer without permission after she has left, she is not in violation.
rationales.C: Contact is not banned outright. What is prohibited is the use of firm records, meaning client lists and other information taken from the former employer; publicly available contact information may be used, subject to any agreement to the contrary, and here no such agreement exists.

questions.stem: Allen, an equity analyst, registers with the government authorities to start a competing investment company. She does the registration on her own time outside the office and seeks no clients for the new company while still employed. Her conduct most likely:

options.A: is permissible preparation to compete.
options.B: requires her employer's written consent.
options.C: violates Standard IV(A) regardless of the timing.

rationales.A: Allen's preparation for the new business by registering with the regulatory authorities does not conflict with the work for her employer if the preparations have been done on Allen's own time outside the office and if Allen will not be soliciting clients for the business or otherwise operating the new company until she has left her current employer. Both conditions hold here.
rationales.B: Preparation of this kind does not require the employer's consent. Consent attaches to rendering compensated outside services and to competing with the employer while still employed, neither of which Allen is doing by filing a registration on her own time.
rationales.C: Registering with the regulatory authorities on her own time is preparation, which is permissible so long as it does not impair the work she does for her employer and she does not solicit clients or operate the new company before leaving. Timing is precisely what distinguishes allowed preparation from a breach of loyalty.

questions.stem: A group of employees plans to resign in a few weeks and believes the new entity it is forming would be qualified to respond to a request for proposal that was sent to their current employer and to all of its competitors. The submission period closes before the resignations take effect. Responding to the request without the employer's permission most likely:

options.A: is permissible, as the request went to all competitors.
options.B: is permissible, as responding is only preparation.
options.C: is a violation, as it competes directly with the employer.

rationales.A: That the request for proposal was distributed to the employer and to all of its competitors makes the process open to the market, not open to the employer's own staff. Responding to the same request while still employed puts the group in direct competition with the employer, and the breadth of the distribution list does not cure that.
rationales.B: An actual bid against the employer is competition, not mere preparation. Registering a future entity or planning on one's own time is preparation; submitting a competing response to a request the employer is answering is the competition itself, and it requires the employer's permission.
rationales.C: A group of employees responding to a request for proposal that their employer is also responding to would lead to direct competition between the employees and the employer. Such conduct violates Standard IV(A) unless the group of employees receives permission from their employer to respond. That the submission period closes before the resignations take effect only confirms that the competition occurs while the duty of loyalty is still owed.

questions.stem: Crome, a private banker, has spent eight years at YBSafe Bank and is hired by a competing bank that pays a substantial signing bonus to advisers who bring their own client portfolios. She plans to solicit 70% of her YBSafe clients to follow her. Most likely, Crome:

options.A: must deliver the client portfolio the bonus paid for.
options.B: may not contact her YBSafe clients even after leaving.
options.C: may contact them after leaving, but not from YBSafe records.

rationales.A: No compensation arrangement with the new employer can override the former employer's ownership of its records. The signing bonus creates an incentive, not a right; client lists remain YBSafe's proprietary information whatever the new bank has agreed to pay.
rationales.B: Contact after termination is permitted. What is prohibited is the use of client records and information built and kept at YBSafe; publicly available information may be used, and any non-compete or non-solicitation terms in her contract would be a separate matter from Standard IV(A).
rationales.C: Crome may contact former clients upon termination of her employment with YBSafe Bank, but she is prohibited from using client records built and kept with her in her capacity as an employee of YBSafe Bank. Client lists are proprietary information of her former employer and must not be used for her own or her new employer's benefit. Use of written, electronic or any other form of records from her prior employer, other than publicly available information, to contact her former clients at YBSafe Bank would be a violation of Standard IV(A).

questions.stem: Webb, whose contract with RSI includes a two-year non-solicitation clause, is terminated by the firm. While at RSI she had connected with clients through her LinkedIn network. Several days after her departure she updates her LinkedIn profile, and LinkedIn automatically sends a notification of the update to her entire network. Webb most likely:

options.A: violated Standard IV(A) by soliciting RSI's clients.
options.B: did not violate Standard IV(A).
options.C: violated Standard IV(A) by staying connected to clients.

rationales.A: An automatic notification generated by LinkedIn after her employment has ended does not amount to solicitation of clients, so treating it as solicitation misapplies Standard IV(A). Webb neither sent the notification nor asked anyone for business.
rationales.B: Webb's actions did not violate Standard IV(A). She updated her LinkedIn profile only after her employment ended, and the updated employment profile notification sent by LinkedIn does not amount to solicitation of clients. Best practice would dictate that Webb maintain separate accounts for her personal and professional social media activities. At a minimum, prior to her departure from the firm, Webb should discuss with RSI how to address any client information contained in her social media networks.
rationales.C: A non-solicitation agreement restricts active solicitation of the employer's clients. It does not require a departing employee to sever existing social media connections or to leave an employment profile unchanged after the employment has ended.

questions.stem: Gupta is a research analyst at NIM, which follows a team-based research process and posts its recommendations on a password-protected client website. Gupta uses his personal blog, which is widely available, to express his own opinions as a counterpoint to NIM's commentary. Gupta most likely:

options.A: complied, as his blog is open to the public.
options.B: complied, as he posted only his personal opinions.
options.C: violated Standard IV(A), as he disclosed firm information.

rationales.A: That the blog is freely available to the general public is the problem rather than the defence. The firm's recommendations are not freely available across the internet, and publishing a counterpoint to them on an open blog discloses them indirectly; the wide availability also does nothing to excuse using firm resources for personal advantage.
rationales.B: Framing the posts as his own opinions does not make them independent of the firm's work. Because the commentary is written as a counterpoint to NIM's recommendations, which sit behind a password-protected client website, the posts indirectly reveal those recommendations, and that is a disclosure of confidential firm information.
rationales.C: Gupta violated Standard IV(A) by disclosing confidential firm information through his personal blog. The recommendations on the firm's website for clients are not freely available across the internet, but his personal blog post indirectly provides the firm's recommendations. In addition, by posting research commentary drawn from a team-based research process on his personal blog, Gupta is using firm resources for his personal advantage.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), independent business activity undertaken while a member is still employed is most likely:

options.A: permitted without employer involvement if conducted outside working hours.
options.B: prohibited outright, whatever is disclosed or consented to.
options.C: permitted, except for services the employer offers, absent consent.

rationales.A: Doing the work after hours does not remove the employer from the picture. A member or candidate who plans to engage in an independent business for compensation while employed must notify the employer and describe the types of services to be rendered to prospective independent clients, the expected duration of those services, and the compensation for them, and must not render services until the employer has consented to all terms of the arrangement. The timing of the work is irrelevant to that requirement; what matters is whether the service competes with, or could deprive, the employer.
rationales.B: Independent business is not precluded by Standard IV(A). Members and candidates are also not prohibited from preparing to enter an independent business, so long as they do not solicit or provide services to clients or otherwise cause harm to the employer. What is prohibited is rendering a service the employer offers without the employer's consent. Notification of the services, their expected duration and the compensation, followed by the employer's consent to all terms, is precisely what makes such an arrangement acceptable, so a blanket prohibition overstates the Standard.
rationales.C: Standard IV(A) does not preclude members or candidates from engaging in an independent business while still employed, but they are prohibited from providing a service offered by their employer without the employer's consent, because such conduct would conflict with the interests of the employer. Members and candidates are not prohibited from preparing to enter into an independent business so long as they do not solicit or provide services to clients or otherwise cause harm to their employer. Those who plan to engage in an independent business for compensation while employed must notify their employer and describe the types of services they will render to prospective independent clients, the expected duration of the services, and the compensation for the services. They must not render services until they receive consent from their employer to all of the terms of the arrangement.

questions.stem: Before terminating the employment relationship, an employee who plans to enter a competitive business is most likely:

options.A: free to prepare, absent a breach of the duty of loyalty.
options.B: free to solicit the employer's clients away from the premises.
options.C: barred from any arrangement to enter that business.

rationales.A: A departing employee is generally free to make arrangements or preparations to go into a competitive business before terminating the relationship with his or her employer, as long as such preparations do not breach the employee's duty of loyalty. Members and candidates who are contemplating seeking other employment must not contact existing or potential clients prior to leaving their employer to discuss a potential change in their employment status. After providing notice of an intent to resign, they may inform the clients with whom they work that they are leaving and going to a new firm, but must not communicate information in a manner that could be seen as explicitly or implicitly soliciting clients or business for the new employer. They may provide the name of the new employer, but must not provide their contact information there before the employment ends without the permission of the current employer, and must not describe the services available at the new firm or otherwise promote it to the current firm's clients without that permission.
rationales.B: Soliciting the employer's clients while still employed breaches the duty of loyalty regardless of where the solicitation occurs; the premises are not the test. Members and candidates contemplating other employment must not contact existing or potential clients before leaving to discuss a change in their employment status, and even after giving notice they may not communicate in a manner that explicitly or implicitly solicits clients or business for the new employer.
rationales.C: Preparation to compete, such as forming an entity or arranging office space, is generally permitted before termination. What is barred is conduct that breaches the duty of loyalty, including soliciting the employer's clients or otherwise causing the employer harm, so an automatic violation on the mere fact of an arrangement is too broad a reading of the Standard.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), acting contrary to an employer's interests is most likely:

options.A: required where clients or market integrity must be protected.
options.B: permitted whenever it advances the member's own position.
options.C: impermissible in all circumstances.

rationales.A: A member's or candidate's personal interests, and those of the employer, are secondary to protecting the integrity of capital markets and the interests of clients. Circumstances may therefore arise, such as when an employer is engaged in illegal or unethical activity, in which members and candidates must act contrary to their employer's interests in order to comply with their duties to the market and to clients. In such instances, certain activities that would normally violate the duty to the employer, such as contradicting employer instructions, violating certain policies and procedures, or preserving a record by copying employer records, may be justified. Such action is permitted only if the intent is clearly aimed at protecting clients or the integrity of the market, not for personal gain.
rationales.B: The whistle-blowing exception exists to protect clients and the integrity of the capital markets, and personal gain is not a qualifying motive. Action against the employer's interests is permitted only where the intent is clearly aimed at that protection, so using a disclosure to strengthen one's own position, for instance a wrongful-dismissal claim, falls outside the exception.
rationales.C: Where the employer is engaged in illegal or unethical activity, the member may be obligated to act against the employer's interests in order to meet duties to clients and to the market. Conduct that would otherwise breach the duty to the employer can be justified in those circumstances, so a rule that never permits it misstates the Standard.

questions.stem: After an employee has left a firm, the skills and experience obtained while employed there are most likely:

options.A: the former employer's confidential property.
options.B: neither confidential nor privileged information.
options.C: usable only after a two-year cooling-off period.

rationales.A: Skills and experience are not confidential or privileged and they travel with the employee. What the firm owns is its work product and records: work performed on behalf of the employer, client lists, and other firm records, whether held as paper copies or electronically on personal devices for the member's convenience, must be returned to the employer or erased unless the firm gives permission to keep them after employment ends. That duty attaches to records, not to what the employee has learned.
rationales.B: Once an employee has left the firm, the skills and experience that the employee obtained while employed are not confidential or privileged information. Similarly, simple knowledge of the names and existence of former clients is generally not confidential unless deemed so by an agreement or by law. Standard IV(A) does not prohibit experience or knowledge gained at one employer from being used at another employer. Work performed on behalf of the employer, client lists, or other firm records, whether stored as paper copies or electronically on personal devices such as phones, tablets or laptops for the member's or candidate's convenience, must be returned to the employer or erased unless the firm gives permission to keep those records after employment ends.
rationales.C: No waiting period applies to the use of one's own skills and experience; Standard IV(A) does not prohibit knowledge gained at one employer from being used at another. Any delay would have to come from a contractual restriction such as a non-compete, not from the Standard itself.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), a member's use of social media for professional purposes is most likely:

options.A: treated no differently from personal use.
options.B: permitted, including firm-approved client-engagement accounts.
options.C: limited to accounts owned by the employer.

rationales.A: The distinction between the two matters. A firm-approved business-related account is part of the firm's assets, which requires the member to transfer or delete it as directed by the firm's policies and procedures, while a purely personal profile carries no such obligation. That is why best practice is to maintain separate accounts for personal and professional social media activity.
rationales.B: Members and candidates may create social media profiles solely for professional reasons, including firm-approved accounts for client engagements. Such firm-approved business-related accounts are part of the firm's assets, which requires members and candidates to transfer or delete the accounts as directed by their firm's policies and procedures. Best practice for members and candidates is to maintain separate accounts for their personal and professional social media activities.
rationales.C: Members and candidates may create professional profiles of their own; the Standard does not confine professional activity to employer-owned accounts. The constraint concerns firm-approved accounts, which are firm assets and must be transferred or deleted as the firm's policies and procedures direct, and compliance with the employer's social media policies generally.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), a member who wishes to undertake independent practice in competition with his employer is most likely:

options.A: barred from any such practice while employed.
options.B: free to proceed with the employer's written consent.
options.C: barred from preparing to compete before terminating.

rationales.A: The Standards do not include a complete prohibition against undertaking independent practice. A member or candidate may undertake independent practice that may result in compensation or other benefit in competition with the employer, so the activity is restricted rather than forbidden, and the restriction is satisfied by obtaining the employer's consent.
rationales.B: Under Standard IV(A) Loyalty, members and candidates may undertake independent practice that may result in compensation or other benefit in competition with their employer as long as they obtain consent from their employer. Written consent is what permits practice that could result in compensation or other benefits in competition with the employer, because it lets the employer weigh the conflict before any service is rendered. Neither a complete prohibition on independent practice nor a bar on preparing to compete is consistent with the Standards.
rationales.C: The Standards allow members and candidates to make arrangements or preparations to go into a competitive business, as long as those arrangements do not interfere with their duty to their current employer. Preparation is therefore permitted before termination; it is conduct that breaches the duty of loyalty, such as soliciting current clients, that is barred.

questions.stem: Jackman is launching an advisory firm and offers a $10,000 incentive to any adviser who joins with at least $200,000 in committed client investments. Consistent with Standard IV(A), the offer is most likely acceptable to:

options.A: no adviser.
options.B: an adviser who discloses it and whose clients switch.
options.C: an adviser who is currently unemployed.

rationales.A: The offer does not directly violate the Code and Standards. An incentive tied to the assets an adviser brings with him is not itself prohibited; what is prohibited is the soliciting an employed adviser would have to do in order to qualify for it. There may be out-of-work members and candidates who can arrange the necessary commitments without violating the Code and Standards, so the offer cannot be condemned as impermissible for everyone.
rationales.B: Standard IV(A) Loyalty governs what is permissible when leaving a current employer, and soliciting clients is strictly prohibited. Assembling $200,000 in committed investments from the clients of a current employer while still employed is inconsistent with the Code and Standards even with the required disclosure; disclosure does not cure the solicitation.
rationales.C: A member or candidate is not eligible for the new position unless he or she is currently unemployed, because soliciting the clients of the member's or candidate's current employer is prohibited. Standard IV(A) Loyalty discusses the activities permissible when leaving a current employer, and soliciting clients is strictly prohibited; an employed adviser could reach the committed-investment threshold only by doing so. The offer itself does not violate the Code and Standards, however, because there may be out-of-work members and candidates who can arrange the necessary commitments without violating it.

questions.stem: After a member gives notice of an intent to resign, the notification of clients and the handling of firm files are most likely governed by:

options.A: local employment law alone.
options.B: the employer's policies and procedures.
options.C: the member's own authorship of the work.

rationales.A: Following the employer's notification and records policies is an obligation under the Code and Standards, not merely a matter of local law. Standard IV(A) independently requires the member to comply with those policies, to refrain from taking records or files without written permission, and to follow the employer's social media policies, including how a departure is disclosed on firm platforms.
rationales.B: Once notice is provided to the employer of the intent to resign, the member or candidate must follow the employer's policies and procedures related to notifying clients of his or her planned departure. In addition, the member or candidate must not take records or files to a new employer without the written permission of the previous employer. Members and candidates also must comply with their employer's policies regarding the use of social media during their employment, including the manner of disclosing their departure on firm social media platforms.
rationales.C: Work performed on behalf of the employer is firm property, and authorship confers no right to take it. Records and files may not be taken to a new employer without the written permission of the previous employer, whether they are held as paper copies or electronically, and regardless of who produced them.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), a member's duty of loyalty to an employer most likely ends:

options.A: when the employment relationship itself ends.
options.B: when the member accepts a written offer elsewhere.
options.C: when the member submits a letter of resignation.

rationales.A: When members and candidates are planning to leave their current employer, they must continue to act in the employer's best interest until the employment relationship ends. A letter of resignation does not necessarily signify the end of the relationship, especially if there is still a period of employment to complete. Generally, the employment relationship ends once the employee is no longer being paid or no longer has responsibilities at the company. Until then, members and candidates must not engage in any activities that could conflict with their duty of loyalty to their employer.
rationales.B: Accepting a future position does not terminate current duties. The member must continue to act in the employer's best interest until the employment relationship actually ends, which generally occurs once the employee is no longer being paid and no longer has responsibilities at the company, not when a new offer is signed.
rationales.C: A letter of resignation does not necessarily signify the end of the relationship, especially if there is still a period of employment to complete. Loyalty continues until the relationship actually ends, generally when compensation and responsibilities cease, so activities that conflict with the duty remain prohibited throughout any notice period.

questions.stem: A client offers to compensate Jurgen, a portfolio manager, beyond the compensation provided by her firm, based on the capital appreciation of his portfolio. Jurgen's most appropriate course of action is to:

options.A: decline, to avoid short-term performance pressure.
options.B: obtain her employer's permission before accepting.
options.C: decline, to avoid conflicts with her other clients.

rationales.A: The arrangement could lead to short-term performance pressure, but that pressure is not an automatic disqualifier and declining is not required. Members and candidates may enter into such agreements as long as they have disclosed the arrangements to their employer and obtained the employer's permission for them.
rationales.B: This involves Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements. An arrangement under which Jurgen would be compensated beyond the compensation provided by her firm, on the basis of an account's performance, is not a violation of the Standards as long as Jurgen discloses the arrangement in writing to her employer and obtains permission from her employer prior to entering into the arrangement. Written disclosure and prior permission are what allow the employer to weigh the conflict with other clients and the short-term performance pressure the arrangement creates.
rationales.C: The private compensation arrangement could conflict with the interests of other clients, but members and candidates may still enter into such agreements provided they disclose the arrangement in writing to the employer and obtain the employer's permission beforehand. The conflict is managed through disclosure and consent rather than by turning the arrangement down.

questions.stem: Jones, a financial adviser, serves on the board of directors of Exercise Unlimited and recommends its stock to clients. Because he receives no monetary compensation for the board service, he makes no disclosure of it. Jones is most likely required to disclose the board seat to:

options.A: no one.
options.B: his employer.
options.C: Exercise Unlimited's shareholders.

rationales.A: The absence of a fee does not remove the duty to disclose. Nonmonetary benefits received for board service can create the same conflicts of interest as cash compensation, and Standard IV(B) requires members and candidates to obtain their employer's consent before accepting compensation or benefits that compete with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest. Nonmonetary compensation may create a conflict of interest in the same manner as being paid to serve as a director.
rationales.B: Jones violated Standard IV(B) by failing to disclose to his employer benefits received in exchange for his services on the board of directors. His service as a board director creates a conflict of interest because he has a personal incentive for recommending Exercise Unlimited stock. Nonmonetary compensation may create a conflict of interest in the same manner as being paid to serve as a director, so the board seat and the benefits flowing from it had to be disclosed to his employer regardless of the fact that no cash changed hands.
rationales.C: The disclosure Standard IV(B) requires runs to Jones's employer, whose consent is what protects against divided loyalties; it is not a duty owed to the shareholders of the company on whose board he sits. Telling Exercise Unlimited's shareholders would leave his employer unaware of the personal incentive behind his buy recommendation and unable to evaluate his actions and motivations.

questions.stem: Hollis gained the appropriate approvals from his employer, Specialty Investment Management, before accepting an invitation to meet ABC Oil's chief executive officer, declined the travel arrangements ABC Oil offered, and on his return disclosed to his employer the dinner he had attended. With respect to Standard IV(B), Hollis most likely:

options.A: violated the standard by accepting an undisclosed benefit.
options.B: did not violate the standard.
options.C: violated the standard by accepting the meeting.

rationales.A: Hollis disclosed his attendance at the dinner to his employer upon his return, so the dinner was not an undisclosed benefit. That disclosure enabled Specialty Investment Management to assess whether the dinner has any impact on future reports and recommendations by Hollis related to ABC Oil, which is precisely the employer assessment Standard IV(B) is designed to permit.
rationales.B: Hollis's actions did not violate Standard IV(B). Through gaining approval before accepting the meeting and declining the offered travel arrangements, Hollis sought to avoid any potential conflicts of interest between his company and ABC Oil. By disclosing the dinner upon his return, Hollis enabled Specialty Investment Management to assess whether it has any impact on future reports and recommendations by Hollis related to ABC Oil.
rationales.C: Meeting with a company's management is ordinary analyst work and is permissible; Standard IV(B) does not require members to avoid such contact. Prior approval from the employer, declining the offered travel arrangements, and disclosing the dinner on return together prevent any violation arising from the meeting itself.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), the written consent a member must obtain from an employer is most likely satisfied by:

options.A: any documentable communication, including a retrievable email.
options.B: a physically signed paper document only.
options.C: the employer's silence after notification.

rationales.A: Written consent includes any form of communication that can be documented, for example communication via email that can be retrieved and documented. The object of the requirement is a durable record that the employer was informed of the arrangement and agreed to it, not any particular medium, so an archived email satisfies the writing requirement.
rationales.B: The requirement is documentation, not paper. Any form of communication that can be documented qualifies, and an email that can be retrieved and documented satisfies the writing requirement, so confining written consent to a physically signed document reads the standard more narrowly than it is written.
rationales.C: Consent must actually be given and must be capable of being documented. Silence produces no record that the employer considered the arrangement and approved it, so it cannot be relied on as written consent under Standard IV(B).

questions.stem: The requirement under Standard IV(B) that members and candidates obtain their employer's permission for additional compensation or benefits is best described as serving to:

options.A: identify arrangements that may compromise loyalty and objectivity.
options.B: let employers recapture outside income earned by employees.
options.C: support the employer's tax reporting.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must obtain permission for additional compensation or benefits because such arrangements may affect loyalties and objectivity and create potential conflicts of interest. Disclosure allows an employer to consider the outside arrangements when evaluating the actions and motivations of members and candidates. Moreover, the employer is entitled to have full knowledge of all compensation and benefit arrangements so as to be able to assess the true cost of the services members or candidates are providing.
rationales.B: The purpose is conflict assessment, because such arrangements may affect loyalties and objectivity, rather than income recapture. Standard IV(B) gives the employer the knowledge it needs to evaluate the member's actions and motivations and to assess the true cost of the services provided; it creates no employer claim on the member's outside earnings.
rationales.C: The rationale is protection of the employer against divided loyalty and impaired objectivity, not tax administration. Standard IV(B) is a professional conduct requirement: the employer must be able to consider outside compensation and benefit arrangements when evaluating a member's actions and motivations and the true cost of the member's services.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), a member or candidate hired by an employer on a part-time or contract basis is most likely:

options.A: required to owe every employer identical full-time duties.
options.B: permitted to work for multiple firms.
options.C: excluded from the scope of Standard IV.

rationales.A: The duties owed to each employer are shaped by the terms of each engagement rather than being an undifferentiated full-time loyalty owed to all of them at once. During the contracting and hiring process, members and candidates should address and negotiate with their employer the parameters around their ability to provide services to other employers that may be competitive with that employer, which is what defines the duty owed in each case.
rationales.B: There may be instances in which a member or candidate is hired by an employer on a part-time or contract basis, allowing the member or candidate to work for multiple firms. During the contracting and hiring process, members and candidates should address and negotiate with their employer the parameters around their ability to provide services to other employers that may be competitive with their employer.
rationales.C: Standard IV applies to part-time and contract engagements as it does to full-time employment. Multi-employer arrangements call for the duties owed to each employer to be defined and agreed, best negotiated up front during contracting and hiring, rather than for such workers to be exempted from employer duties.

questions.stem: Mattock, senior vice president and head of research at H&V, is responsible for the firm's compliance procedures for disseminating research. She changes her recommendation on Timber Products from buy to sell and advises other H&V executives; her subordinate Frampton immediately sells Timber Products for himself and for his clients, and other personnel inform institutional customers before the change is publicly disseminated. Mattock most likely:

options.A: committed no violation.
options.B: violated Standard IV(C).
options.C: violated Standard II(A) only.

rationales.A: Advising selected executives and clients ahead of public dissemination is not proper notification and compounds the problem rather than curing it. As the person responsible for the firm's dissemination procedures, Mattock's failure to reasonably and adequately supervise the actions of those accountable to her is itself the violation of Standard IV(C).
rationales.B: Mattock violated Standard IV(C) by failing to reasonably and adequately supervise the actions of those accountable to her. In her role as senior vice president and head of research, she must ensure that her firm has procedures for reviewing or recording any trading in the stock of a corporation that has been the subject of an unpublished change in recommendation. If adequate procedures had been established and followed, subordinates would have been informed of their duties, which would have facilitated detection of the improper sales by Frampton and prevented selected disclosure of the recommendation to clients.
rationales.C: The selective disclosure and tipping problem is real, but it is not the only standard engaged, and it is not the conduct tested here. What Mattock is responsible for is her supervisory failure under Standard IV(C): she had to ensure the firm had procedures for reviewing or recording trading in a stock subject to an unpublished change in recommendation, and she did not.

questions.stem: Mason, a vice president at Wheeler responsible for compliance in the trading department, receives part of her compensation based on the department's commission revenues. She notices suspicious purchase orders in Highland stock, which is not on the firm's recommended list, entered by Edwards, a trainee, and takes no action. Mason most likely:

options.A: committed no violation.
options.B: was excused from close review by her commission-based pay.
options.C: violated Standard IV(C).

rationales.A: A supervisor's duty under Standard IV(C) extends to the actions of subordinates, so misconduct by a trainee that adequate review and investigation would have caught is the supervisor's failure as well as the trainee's. Mason noticed the Highland orders and neither reviewed nor investigated them, which is the breach, whoever entered the orders.
rationales.B: Self-interest in the commission revenues aggravates the failure to review and investigate rather than excusing it. Supervisors must be especially sensitive to actual or potential conflicts between their own self-interests and their supervisory responsibilities, so compensation tied to trading revenue calls for more scrutiny of revenue-producing trades, not less.
rationales.C: Mason's failure to adequately review and investigate purchase orders in Highland stock executed by Edwards and her failure to supervise the trainee's activities violate Standard IV(C). Supervisors must be especially sensitive to actual or potential conflicts between their own self-interests and their supervisory responsibilities, and here part of Mason's compensation depended on the commission revenues the trades generated.

questions.stem: Claudius assigns Tabbing to manage both the fund and the CEPSP portfolios. Tabbing places S&P 500 futures orders without designating the account beforehand and assigns the favorable executions to CEPSP after seeing how the market moved. Crozet, the firm, has no written operating procedures and no compliance manual for futures trading. Claudius most likely:

options.A: violated the standard by the dual assignment alone.
options.B: did not violate the standard.
options.C: violated the standard by failing to supervise the futures trading.

rationales.A: Assigning one manager to both portfolios is permissible and is not what the standard prohibits. The violation is the absence of recordkeeping and reporting procedures and the failure to supervise Tabbing's trading: a dual assignment run under adequate procedures requiring the account to be designated before the order is placed would not have allowed the favorable executions to be allocated after the fact.
rationales.B: A supervisor's failure to establish recordkeeping and reporting procedures violates Standard IV(C) whether or not the supervisor knew of the specific improper allocations. Claudius must make a reasonable effort to determine that adequate compliance procedures covering all employee trading activity are established, documented, communicated, and followed, and Crozet had no written operating procedures or compliance manual for futures trading at all.
rationales.C: Claudius violated Standard IV(C) by failing to adequately supervise Tabbing with respect to her S&P 500 trading. He further violated Standard IV(C) by failing to establish recordkeeping and reporting procedures to prevent or detect Tabbing's violations. Claudius must make a reasonable effort to determine that adequate compliance procedures covering all employee trading activity are established, documented, communicated, and followed.

questions.stem: Rasmussen, a trader, observes that her firm's hedge fund performance does not reflect a market decline. She raises the issue with her supervisor, Blair, who tells her not to ask questions, and then with the compliance officer, Saunders, who tells her not to pursue it. Under Standard IV(C), responsibility for reviewing Rasmussen's concerns most likely rests with:

options.A: the fund administrator.
options.B: Rasmussen alone.
options.C: Blair and Saunders.

rationales.A: Whoever calculates or administers the fund's reported performance, a supervisor and a compliance officer presented with credible concerns about that performance have the responsibility to review them. The duty cannot be passed to a service provider, and dismissing the question is itself the failure under Standard IV(C), which obliges supervisors to investigate potential misconduct.
rationales.B: Rasmussen acted properly in bringing her concerns about potential misconduct to supervisory personnel, and doing so discharged her own obligation. The duty tested here is the one owed by Blair and Saunders: supervisors have the responsibility of establishing and encouraging an ethical culture in the firm and of investigating potential misconduct brought to their attention.
rationales.C: Under Standard IV(C), Blair and Saunders, the supervisor and the compliance officer, have the responsibility to review the concerns brought forth by Rasmussen. Supervisors have the responsibility of establishing and encouraging an ethical culture in the firm and investigating potential misconduct. The dismissal of Rasmussen's question violates Standard IV(C) and undermines the firm's ethical operations.

questions.stem: Graf hires Burdette to expand FIM's social media presence at a time when the firm has not yet established policies for online communications. Burdette posts a summary of the firm's buy recommendation for Sun Drive on her personal social media accounts. Graf most likely:

options.A: bears no responsibility for Burdette's posts.
options.B: violated Standard IV(C).
options.C: was excused by the absence of a social media policy.

rationales.A: Graf's failure to establish reasonable procedures for online communications makes him liable under Standard IV(C) even though the posts appeared on Burdette's own accounts. The appropriate business use of personal social media networks is exactly what those procedures and the related employee training have to address, so the personal nature of the accounts does not remove his responsibility.
rationales.B: Graf violated Standard IV(C) by failing to reasonably supervise Burdette with respect to her actions. He did not establish reasonable procedures to prevent the unauthorized dissemination of company research through social media networks. Graf must make sure all employees receive regular training about FIM's policies and procedures, including the appropriate business use of personal social media networks.
rationales.C: The failure to establish that policy is precisely the supervisory violation rather than an excuse for it. A supervisor who hires an employee to expand the firm's social media presence must first establish reasonable procedures to prevent unauthorized dissemination of company research, and must document and communicate them to employees before the activity begins.

questions.stem: Bartlett is the compliance officer for all branches of FFWM. Sokol, a branch adviser, recommends a complex feeder fund to more than 100 retail clients without adequately assessing suitability, and those clients lose $16 million. Bartlett has most likely:

options.A: violated Standard III(C).
options.B: violated Standard IV(C).
options.C: violated none of the Standards.

rationales.A: The suitability breach was Sokol's: Sokol made the recommendations without assessing whether the feeder fund suited each client. Bartlett's failing is a supervisory one under Standard IV(C) — inadequate policies, procedures, training, and supervision — and a compliance officer does not acquire Sokol's Standard III(C) duty to the individual clients by failing to supervise.
rationales.B: Bartlett's actions violated Standard IV(C). Bartlett's inadequate policies, procedures, training, and supervision allowed Sokol to recommend the feeder fund without properly assessing whether the investment was suitable for each client. Bartlett failed to supervise Sokol and failed to adopt and implement written policies and procedures for FFWM designed to prevent investment advisory representatives at FFWM from recommending complex financial products to clients when they are not suitable.
rationales.C: Sokol's own violation does not absolve Bartlett. Bartlett's inadequate policies, training, and supervision are an independent violation of Standard IV(C), which exists precisely so that unsuitable recommendations by advisers are prevented and detected. As compliance officer for every branch, Bartlett had the employees in question subject to his control or influence and so bore supervisory responsibility for them.

questions.stem: D'Addario provides artificially inflated price quotes for mortgage-backed securities to Amity Point in exchange for its securities trades. Bartolucci, the CEO, knows D'Addario provides the quotes but develops no policies or procedures governing them. Bartolucci has most likely:

options.A: failed to retain records of the price quotes.
options.B: committed no violation, having given no quotes.
options.C: failed to adopt and train staff on quote policies.

rationales.A: Nothing in the facts turns on the retention of records. The defect is the absence of policies governing the provision of price quotes to customers and the absence of training on them, which is a failure to supervise under Standard IV(C) rather than a records failure under Standard V(C).
rationales.B: Personal participation in the inflated quotes is not required for a supervisory violation. As CEO, Bartolucci knew that D'Addario was providing price quotes and still failed to develop, promote, and train employees on adequate policies governing those quotes, and failed to supervise D'Addario so as to prevent and detect the illegal and unethical activity.
rationales.C: Bartolucci's conduct violated Standard IV(C) by failing to develop, promote, and train employees on adequate policies governing the provision of price quotes to their customers. Bartolucci failed to supervise D'Addario to prevent and detect D'Addario's illegal and unethical activities. The knowledge that quotes were being provided at all is what made the absence of any governing policy and training a supervisory failure.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), whether an investment professional has supervisory responsibility is most likely determined by:

options.A: formal designation as the firm's compliance officer.
options.B: the membership status of the employees supervised.
options.C: control or influence over employees.

rationales.A: Supervisory responsibility is not confined to the holder of the compliance title. Any investment professional who has employees subject to his or her control or influence exercises supervisory responsibility, so a line manager cannot point at the compliance officer to escape the duty.
rationales.B: Supervisory responsibility applies whether or not the supervised employees are CFA Institute members, CFA charterholders, or candidates in the CFA Program. The status of the people supervised is irrelevant; what creates the duty is the supervisor's control or influence over them.
rationales.C: Any investment professional who has employees subject to her or his control or influence — whether or not the employees are CFA Institute members, CFA charterholders, or candidates in the CFA Program — exercises supervisory responsibility under Standard IV(C). The test is the existence of control or influence over employees, not a job title and not the credentials of the staff.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), delegation of supervisory duties is most likely:

options.A: permitted, with instruction of the delegates.
options.B: prohibited for members and candidates.
options.C: permitted, with responsibility passing to the delegates.

rationales.A: Members and candidates with oversight responsibilities for large numbers of employees may not be able to personally evaluate the conduct of these employees on a continuing basis. These members and candidates may delegate supervisory duties to subordinates who directly oversee the other employees. A member's or candidate's responsibilities under Standard IV(C) include instructing those subordinates to whom supervision is delegated about methods to promote compliance, including preventing and detecting violations of laws, rules, regulations, firm policies, and the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: Delegation is permitted, and at scale it is necessary, because a supervisor of a large staff cannot personally evaluate every employee's conduct on a continuing basis. What Standard IV(C) adds is a condition rather than a prohibition: the subordinates to whom supervision is delegated must be instructed about the methods for promoting compliance and for preventing and detecting violations.
rationales.C: Delegation moves the day-to-day oversight, not the ultimate responsibility. The delegating member remains responsible under Standard IV(C) and must instruct the delegates about methods to promote compliance, including preventing and detecting violations of laws, rules, regulations, firm policies, and the Code and Standards.

questions.stem: A member with supervisory responsibility who finds the firm's compliance system inadequate is most likely required to:

options.A: quietly compensate for the gaps through personal vigilance.
options.B: accept the supervisory duties without objection.
options.C: notify senior management and recommend corrections.

rationales.A: Extra personal vigilance leaves the defective system in place for everyone else and for the member's successor, and keeping the defect quiet denies the firm the chance to repair it. The standard requires escalation: the inadequacy goes to the firm's senior managers together with recommended corrective action.
rationales.B: Simply accepting the role is not the response required. The member must bring the inadequacy to the attention of senior managers and recommend corrective action, and where supervisory responsibilities clearly cannot be discharged because the compliance system is absent or inadequate, the member should decline to accept supervisory responsibility until reasonable procedures are adopted.
rationales.C: A member or candidate with supervisory responsibility must bring an inadequate compliance system to the attention of the firm's senior managers and recommend corrective action. If the member or candidate clearly cannot discharge supervisory responsibilities because of the absence of a compliance system or because of an inadequate compliance system, the member or candidate should decline to accept supervisory responsibility until the firm adopts reasonable procedures to allow adequate exercise of supervisory responsibility. That is what Standard IV(C) requires of the supervisor.

questions.stem: A supervisor who learns that an employee may have violated the law or acted unethically is most likely required to:

options.A: rely on the employee's assurances.
options.B: promptly assess the extent of the wrongdoing.
options.C: note the incident at the annual review.

rationales.A: Relying on an employee's statements about the extent of the violation, or on assurances that the wrongdoing will not reoccur, is not enough. The supervisor must promptly initiate an assessment of how far the wrongdoing extends and, pending its outcome, take steps to ensure the violation is not repeated, such as placing limits on the employee's activities or increasing monitoring of them.
rationales.B: Once a supervisor learns that an employee has violated or may have violated the law or engaged in unethical behavior, Standard IV(C) requires the supervisor to promptly initiate an assessment to determine the extent of the wrongdoing. Relying on an employee's statements about the extent of the violation or assurances that the wrongdoing will not reoccur is not enough. Reporting the misconduct to the appropriate compliance and management personnel and warning the employee to cease the activity are also not enough. Pending the outcome of the investigation, a supervisor must take steps to ensure that the violation will not be repeated, such as placing limits on the employee's activities or increasing the monitoring of the employee's activities.
rationales.C: A notation in a performance review is neither the prompt investigation nor the interim control the standard requires. Reporting the misconduct to compliance and management and warning the employee to cease are themselves not enough; the supervisor must assess the extent of the wrongdoing and restrict or monitor the employee while that assessment is pending.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), members and candidates with supervisory responsibility are most likely required to:

options.A: make reasonable efforts to detect violations.
options.B: delegate the detection of violations to internal audit.
options.C: make reasonable efforts only once a violation is reported.

rationales.A: Members and candidates with supervisory responsibility must also make reasonable efforts to detect violations of laws, rules, regulations, and firm policies as well as unethical behavior. Supervisors exercise reasonable supervision by establishing and implementing written compliance procedures and ensuring that those procedures are followed through periodic review. If a member or candidate has adopted reasonable procedures and taken steps to institute an effective compliance program, then the member or candidate may not be in violation of Standard IV(C) if he or she does not detect violations that occur despite these efforts; the fact that violations do occur may indicate, however, that the compliance procedures are inadequate. Merely enacting procedures may not be sufficient, and members may violate the standard if they know or should know that the procedures are not being followed.
rationales.B: Internal audit may assist, but the detection duty belongs to those with supervisory responsibility over the employees concerned, and handing it to another function does not discharge it. The supervisor discharges it by establishing and implementing written compliance procedures and ensuring through periodic review that the procedures are actually followed.
rationales.C: Reasonable efforts to detect violations are owed before anything is reported, not only in response to a report. Detection is exercised through written compliance procedures and periodic review of whether they are being followed; a supervisor who knows or should know the procedures are not being followed may violate the standard even if nothing has been reported.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), an employer's policies governing the employer-employee relationship are most likely:

options.A: binding on members unless they conflict with law or the Code.
options.B: binding on the firm rather than on its individual members.
options.C: binding on members even where they conflict with law or the Code.

rationales.A: Implicit in Standard IV(A) is the obligation of members and candidates to comply with the policies and procedures established by their employers that govern the employer-employee relationship — to the extent that such policies and procedures do not conflict with applicable laws, rules, and regulations or the Code and Standards. The duty of loyalty therefore reaches the employer's own rules, but it stops where those rules would require unlawful conduct or a breach of the Code.
rationales.B: The obligation to comply with the employer's governing policies and procedures is implicit in the member's own duty of loyalty under Standard IV(A). A firm's code of ethics is not addressed only to the entity: a member who disregards it breaches the standard, whatever the firm's separate obligations may be.
rationales.C: The obligation runs only to lawful policies. It applies to the extent that the employer's policies and procedures do not conflict with applicable laws, rules, and regulations or the Code and Standards, so loyalty never shelters a directive that would require a violation of either.

questions.stem: Standard IV(A)'s duty of loyalty, as it bears on a member's life outside work, is most likely:

options.A: extended to the member's private family and financial decisions.
options.B: bounded by important personal and family obligations.
options.C: owed ahead of personal interests in every matter.

rationales.A: Standard IV(A) governs conduct in and related to the employment relationship. Personal matters that are unrelated to that relationship sit outside the duty of loyalty, so the standard does not reach into a member's private family decisions or personal financial choices. Where such matters begin to interfere with the member's work on a regular or significant basis, the response called for is a dialogue with the employer about balancing the two, not an extension of the employer's claim over the member's private life.
rationales.B: Standard IV(A) is not meant to be a blanket requirement to place employer interests ahead of personal interests in all matters. The standard does not require members and candidates to subordinate important personal and family obligations to their work. The guidance instead directs that members and candidates should enter into a dialogue with their employer about balancing personal and employment obligations when personal matters may interfere with their work on a regular or significant basis. The duty of loyalty is therefore bounded: it is owed in matters related to employment, and it coexists with the member's legitimate personal and family commitments rather than extinguishing them.
rationales.C: This overstates the standard. Standard IV(A) governs matters related to employment; it is not a blanket requirement to place employer interests ahead of personal interests in all matters, and it does not require members and candidates to subordinate important personal and family obligations to their work. Reading the standard as an absolute subordination in every matter would oblige a member to sacrifice family and personal duties that the guidance expressly preserves.

questions.stem: The duty of loyalty under Standard IV(A), for a member who may be an employee or an independent contractor, is most likely:

options.A: confined to salaried employees and never to contract work.
options.B: identical for both, regardless of what the governing agreement provides.
options.C: owed in both, with contractor duties set by the agreement.

rationales.A: Standard IV(A) is not confined to salaried employees. A wide variety of business relationships exists in the investment industry, and a member or candidate may be an employee or an independent contractor. The standard applies in the employment context, and it can reach an independent-contractor relationship, where the member's duties are governed by the oral or written agreement with the client. Because of that, the member must first determine which status applies rather than assume the standard is irrelevant to contract work.
rationales.B: The duties are not identical irrespective of the agreement. An independent contractor's duties are governed by the oral or written agreement between the member and the client, so the terms of that agreement, not an employee template, define what is owed. Members and candidates should take care to clearly define the scope of their responsibilities and the expectations of each client in the context of each relationship; once the relationship is established, the member has a duty to abide by the terms of the agreement.
rationales.C: Standard IV(A) applies in the employment context. A wide variety of business relationships exists in the investment industry; for instance, a member or candidate may be an employee or an independent contractor. Members and candidates must determine whether they are employees or independent contractors in order to determine the applicability of Standard IV(A). Duties in an independent contractor relationship are governed by the oral or written agreement between the member and the client. Members and candidates should take care to clearly define the scope of their responsibilities and the expectations of each client in the context of each relationship, and once a member or candidate establishes a relationship with a client, he or she has a duty to abide by the terms of the agreement.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), promoting the services of a new firm to current clients before a member's employment ends is most likely:

options.A: prohibited, even to protect client interests.
options.B: permitted if clients ask unprompted.
options.C: permitted if clients would benefit.

rationales.A: Standard IV(A) guidance on leaving an employer is explicit on this point: 'Members and candidates cannot promote the services of a new firm in the name of protecting the interests of clients until their employment with their current firm ends. Members and candidates who believe the conduct or business practices of their employer are so egregious that they harm client interests are free to resign their position and subsequently notify their former clients or other appropriate parties of their concerns.' Client protection is therefore not a defense to pre-departure promotion. Where an employer's conduct or business practices genuinely harm clients, the permitted sequence is to resign first and only then notify former clients or other appropriate parties of the concern.
rationales.B: A client's unprompted question does not open the door to promotion. A member who is asked may state facts, such as the name of the new employer, but may not describe or otherwise promote the new firm's services to the current firm's clients while still employed there.
rationales.C: A genuine belief that clients would be better off does not authorize promotion before departure. The duty of loyalty under Standard IV(A) runs until employment with the current firm ends, and only after that point may the member promote or solicit.

questions.stem: When leaving an employer, the activity most likely to violate Standard IV(A) is:

options.A: preparing in good faith to compete.
options.B: using skills acquired at the former employer.
options.C: using the employer's trade secrets without authorization.

rationales.A: Preparation to establish a competing business, undertaken in good faith, is generally permitted while still employed and does not by itself violate Standard IV(A). What the duty of loyalty bars is misuse of the employer's property and information and solicitation of its clients, not the act of planning to compete.
rationales.B: General skills and experience acquired in the course of employment are neither confidential nor privileged, and a departing member may use them at a new employer. Only the employer's own property is protected: trade secrets, confidential information, firm property, and client lists.
rationales.C: Standard IV(A) guidance lists the activities that may constitute a violation: 'unauthorized use of trade secrets; misuse of confidential information, explicit or implicit solicitation of an employer's clients, or promotion of a new employer prior to cessation of employment; self-dealing (appropriating for one's own benefit property, a business opportunity, or information belonging to one's employer); unauthorized use of any firm property, including clients or client lists; and discussing a change in employment in a manner that disparages or denigrates the current employer such that it could cause harm to the firm's interests.' Unauthorized use of trade secrets heads that list, and the common thread running through all of the listed activities is the appropriation or misuse of something that belongs to the employer.

questions.stem: Before a departing member's employment ends, Standard IV(A) most likely permits the member to give clients:

options.A: the new employer's name only.
options.B: the new employer's name and contact details.
options.C: neither the name nor the contact details.

rationales.A: Standard IV(A) guidance on leaving an employer draws the line at identification rather than contact: 'For instance, while they may provide the name of their new employer, members and candidates must not provide their contact information at their new employer before their employment ends without permission of their current employer. They also must not describe to clients the services available at the new firm or in other ways implicitly or explicitly promote their new employer to their current firm's clients without the permission of their current employer.' The name of the new employer is a fact; contact details, a description of the new firm's services, and any other implicit or explicit promotion require the current employer's permission.
rationales.B: Contact information at the new firm goes beyond the permitted disclosure of the employer's name and functions as implicit promotion or solicitation of the current firm's clients. Absent the current employer's permission, it may not be given out during the notice period.
rationales.C: This understates what is allowed. The guidance expressly permits a departing member to provide the name of the new employer; it is the contact details at that employer, and any description or promotion of its services, that must wait for the current employer's permission or for employment to end.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), effective compliance procedures are most likely:

options.A: adopted after a violation reveals a gap.
options.B: designed to anticipate every possible violation.
options.C: in place before a violation occurs.

rationales.A: Procedures written only after a violation has exposed a specific gap come too late to be effective. The requirement is preventive rather than reactive: the procedures must already be in place when the legal or ethical violation would otherwise occur.
rationales.B: Anticipating every potential violation is not the standard, and failing that test does not make a program ineffective. Procedures cannot be designed to cover every possibility; they should instead be designed to anticipate the activities most likely to result in misconduct.
rationales.C: Standard IV(C) guidance on the system for supervision sets out both the timing and the design test: 'To be effective, compliance procedures must be in place prior to the occurrence of a legal or ethical violation. Although compliance procedures cannot be designed to anticipate every potential violation, they should be designed to anticipate the activities most likely to result in misconduct. Compliance programs must be appropriate for the size and nature of the organization. The member or candidate should review model compliance procedures or other industry resources to ensure that the firm's procedures are adequate.' Adequacy therefore has three dimensions: the procedures exist before the fact, they are aimed at the highest-risk activities, and they are scaled to the size and nature of the organization, with model procedures or other industry resources used as a benchmark.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), an effective compliance system most likely consists of:

options.A: a code of ethics alone.
options.B: a code of ethics plus policies, procedures, and review.
options.C: compliance with securities laws alone.

rationales.A: A code of ethics on its own is not an effective compliance system. Drafting the code is only the first element; the system must also establish policies and procedures to achieve compliance with it and with applicable law, and it must review employee actions to see whether the rules are being followed.
rationales.B: Standard IV(C) guidance states the minimum: 'At a minimum, Standard IV(C) requires that members and candidates with supervisory responsibility make reasonable efforts to prevent and detect violations by ensuring the establishment of effective compliance systems. An effective compliance system goes beyond enacting a code of ethics; it also includes establishing policies and procedures to achieve compliance with the code and applicable law and reviewing employee actions to determine whether they are following the rules.' Three components therefore have to be present: the code itself, the policies and procedures that operationalize it alongside applicable law, and the ongoing review of employee conduct that lets the supervisor detect, as well as prevent, violations.
rationales.C: Adherence to applicable securities law is only part of what is required. An effective system goes beyond legal compliance to include a code of ethics, the policies and procedures that implement the code and the law, and review of employee actions against those rules.

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Code and Standards
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard IV: Duties to Employers

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), an employer's authority to set conduct rules for its employees most likely extends to:

options.A: only the policies that regulation requires.
options.B: its own codes of conduct and operating procedures.
options.C: everything except services offered outside the firm.

rationales.A: Employers are not confined to what regulation mandates. They may establish their own codes of conduct and operating procedures, and the member's obligation is to understand those policies fully and confirm that they do not conflict with the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: Standard IV(A) compliance practices place the burden of understanding firm policy on the member: 'Employers may establish codes of conduct and operating procedures for their employees to follow. Members and candidates should fully understand those policies and procedures to ensure that they are not in conflict with the Code and Standards. Members and candidates must understand any restrictions placed by the employer on offering similar services outside the firm while employed by the firm.' That understanding has two purposes: to follow the employer's rules, and to identify any point at which those rules would conflict with the Code and Standards. It also reaches outside service, where the firm's policy may set out a procedure for requesting approval or may prohibit such service outright.
rationales.C: Outside service is not carved out of the employer's authority. The employer may restrict, or require approval for, similar services offered outside the firm while the member is employed there, and the member must understand any such restriction; the policy may outline an approval procedure or be a strict prohibition.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), understanding an employer's termination policies is most likely:

options.A: recommended for every member and candidate.
options.B: necessary only under a non-compete agreement.
options.C: relevant only to human resources staff.
