rationales.A: Standard IV(A) compliance practices: 'Members and candidates should clearly understand the termination policies of their employer, including those that relate to the resignation process, how the termination will be disclosed to clients and staff, and whether updates posted through social media will be allowed.' The recommendation is addressed to the member, not to the firm, and it reaches past the mechanics of resigning to how the departure is communicated: what clients and staff are told, by whom, and whether the member may post about the move on social media. Knowing those rules before resigning is what keeps an otherwise permissible departure from becoming solicitation or disparagement of the former employer.
rationales.B: The recommendation applies to all members and candidates, whether or not their employment agreement contains a non-compete clause. The resignation process, the disclosure of the departure to clients and staff, and any limits on social media posts arise on every departure.
rationales.C: Termination policies are not a human resources matter alone. The departing member is the one who has to follow the resignation process and respect the firm's rules on how the departure is disclosed to clients and staff and on social media use, so the member should clearly understand them.

questions.stem: Regarding their firm's whistleblowing policies, members and candidates are most likely advised to:

options.A: leave the subject to compliance officers.
options.B: discourage formal whistleblowing programs.
options.C: know the policies and encourage best practices.

rationales.A: Awareness of the firm's whistleblowing policies is not delegated to the compliance function. Members and candidates themselves should know what those policies provide, since they are the people who may need to use the reporting channels.
rationales.B: The advice runs in the opposite direction: members and candidates should encourage their firms to adopt industry best practices for whistleblowing rather than resist them, and in many jurisdictions such programs are not optional in any case.
rationales.C: Standard IV(A) compliance practices: 'Members and candidates should be aware of their firm's policies related to whistle-blowing and encourage their firms to adopt industry best practices in this area. Many firms are required by regulatory mandates to establish confidential and anonymous reporting procedures that allow employees to report potentially unethical and illegal activities in the firm.' The recommendation has two parts, awareness and advocacy. Awareness matters because a member who does not know the firm's reporting channel cannot use it; advocacy matters because confidential and anonymous procedures are what make it realistic for an employee to report potentially unethical or illegal activity, and regulatory mandates already require such procedures at many firms.

questions.stem: With respect to giving an employer a copy of the Code and Standards, members and candidates are most likely:

options.A: prohibited from doing so.
options.B: encouraged to do so.
options.C: required to obtain approval first.

rationales.A: Nothing prohibits a member from sharing the Code and Standards with an employer. The opposite is true: providing a copy is encouraged, precisely so the employer learns what obligations the member carries.
rationales.B: Standard IV(A) guidance: 'Members and candidates are encouraged to provide their employers with a copy of the Code and Standards. These materials will inform the employer of the responsibilities of a CFA Institute member or candidate in the CFA Program. The Code and Standards also serve as a basis for questioning employer policies and practices that conflict with these responsibilities.' The recommendation serves two ends. It puts the employer on notice of duties the member cannot set aside, and it gives the member an authoritative reference to point to when a firm policy or practice would conflict with those duties.
rationales.C: Adherence to the Code and Standards is a condition of membership and candidacy and is never conditioned on an employer's approval. The materials are instead a basis for questioning employer policies and practices that conflict with the member's responsibilities.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), the duties created by the employer-employee relationship most likely fall on:

options.A: the employee alone.
options.B: both parties.
options.C: charterholding employees only.

rationales.A: Loyalty does not run in one direction only. The relationship imposes duties on the employer as well, including the duty to provide a positive working environment, and that environment includes an ethical workplace.
rationales.B: Standard IV(A) guidance: 'The employer-employee relationship imposes duties and responsibilities on both parties. Employers must recognize the duties and responsibilities that they owe to their employees if they expect to have contented and productive employees. The employer is also responsible for a positive working environment, which includes an ethical workplace.' The employee's duty of loyalty is therefore only one side of the relationship. Employers that recognize what they owe their employees are the ones likely to have contented and productive staff, and the employer carries responsibility for a working environment that is ethical as well as positive.
rationales.C: The mutual duties arise from the employment relationship itself, not from an employee's charter status. The employer owes its obligations, including an ethical workplace, to all of its employees.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), an employer's policies on the use of social media with clients are most likely to:

options.A: yield to client convenience as advisory guidance.
options.B: bind only the firm's marketing personnel.
options.C: require compliance from every member who uses them.

rationales.A: Firm social media policies are not advisory. Members and candidates must understand and abide by all applicable firm policies and regulations as to the acceptable use of social media to interact with clients and prospective clients. Client convenience is not a ground for departing from them; communications through social media platforms that potentially reach current clients must adhere to the employer's policies and procedures, including those on notification of departing employees.
rationales.B: The obligation is not confined to marketing staff. It attaches to every member and candidate who uses social media to interact with clients and prospective clients, because any such communication can reach current clients and so falls within the employer's policies and procedures. The requirement is especially important when a member or candidate is planning to leave an employer, a situation that arises for investment professionals of every function, not only marketing.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must understand and abide by all applicable firm policies and regulations as to the acceptable use of social media to interact with clients and prospective clients. This requirement is especially important when a member or candidate is planning to leave an employer, because social media use makes determining how and when departure notification is delivered to clients more complex. Communications through social media platforms that potentially reach current clients must adhere to the employer's policies and procedures regarding notification of departing employees.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), a member's duty to an employer before taking on an independent business for compensation is most likely to:

options.A: extend to the services, duration, and compensation.
options.B: stop at bare notice of the plan, leaving out its terms.
options.C: arise only where the employer's own clients are served.

rationales.A: Members and candidates who plan to engage in an independent business for compensation while employed must notify their employer and describe the types of services they will render to prospective independent clients, the expected duration of the services, and the compensation for the services. They must not render services until they receive consent from their employer to all of the terms of the arrangement. Notification and a full description are therefore the first step, and consent to every term is the condition for proceeding.
rationales.B: A bare heads-up is not sufficient. The notification must describe the arrangement: the types of services the member will render to prospective independent clients, the expected duration of those services, and the compensation for them. Without that description the employer cannot evaluate the arrangement, and the member must not render services until the employer has consented to all of the terms.
rationales.C: The duty is not limited to independent work that touches the employer's existing clients. It attaches to any plan to engage in an independent business for compensation while employed, whoever the prospective independent clients are, and the member must not render services until the employer consents to all of the terms of the arrangement.

questions.stem: On leaving an employer, the records a member must return or erase absent the firm's permission to keep them are most likely:

options.A: all firm records, whatever the medium.
options.B: only paper files held in the employer's offices.
options.C: only records the employer requests in writing.

rationales.A: Work performed on behalf of the employer, client lists, or other firm records, whether stored as paper copies or electronically on personal devices such as phones, tablets, or laptop computers for the member's or candidate's convenience, must be returned to the employer or erased unless the firm gives permission to keep those records after employment ends. The medium is irrelevant and the obligation is the default: retention requires the firm's permission.
rationales.B: Office paper files are not the limit of the obligation. Firm records stored electronically on personal devices such as phones, tablets, or laptop computers, held there for the member's own convenience, must equally be returned to the employer or erased unless the firm gives permission to keep them after employment ends.
rationales.C: No written request from the employer is needed to trigger the duty. Work performed on behalf of the employer, client lists, and other firm records must be returned or erased by default; it is permission to keep them, not a demand for their return, that the firm must supply.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(A), agreements that restrict a departing employee's later conduct are most likely to:

options.A: fall outside the duties a member owes under the Code of Ethics.
options.B: bind the member after the employment relationship ends.
options.C: yield to a charterholder's right to practice freely.

rationales.A: Such agreements cannot be disregarded. Members and candidates should take care to review the terms of any post-employment agreement when leaving an employer to determine what, if any, conduct those agreements may prohibit. Breaching a valid agreement can implicate both the governing law and the member's duty of loyalty to the former employer, so the agreement bears directly on conduct under the Code.
rationales.B: Employers may require employees to sign agreements that preclude departing employees from engaging in certain conduct after they have left the firm. Members and candidates should take care to review the terms of any such agreement when leaving their employer to determine what, if any, conduct those agreements may prohibit. The duty of loyalty under Standard IV(A) generally ends with the employment relationship, but a non-solicitation or similar post-employment agreement can extend specific restrictions beyond it, and the member is expected to know which restrictions apply before acting.
rationales.C: Holding the charter confers no immunity from valid contractual restrictions. Employers may require employees to sign agreements precluding certain conduct after departure, and members and candidates should review the terms of any such agreement to determine what conduct it prohibits rather than assume that holding the charter leaves them free to practice as they wish.

questions.stem: For a member's social media activity under Standard IV(A), best practice is most likely to:

options.A: keep personal and professional social media accounts separate.
options.B: avoid professional use of social media.
options.C: combine personal and professional activity in one account.

rationales.A: Best practice for members and candidates is to maintain separate accounts for their personal and professional social media activities. Separation keeps client contacts and firm-related communications identifiable as the employer's, which matters most on departure: at a minimum, before leaving the firm, a member should discuss with the employer how to address any client information contained in his or her social media networks.
rationales.B: Professional use of social media is accepted, not discouraged. The guidance concerns how it is used: members and candidates must understand and abide by all applicable firm policies and regulations on the acceptable use of social media with clients and prospective clients, and best practice is to keep personal and professional accounts separate.
rationales.C: Consolidation is the opposite of the recommended practice. Best practice is to maintain separate accounts for personal and professional social media activities, so that firm and client information does not become entangled with the member's private network, and before departing a member should discuss with the employer how to address any client information held in those networks.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), a member's disclosure of compensation proposed in addition to that received from the employer is most likely:

options.A: made to a supervisor or compliance officer.
options.B: required only above the member's base salary.
options.C: complete once any colleague at the firm has been told.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must disclose to their employer, through their supervisor or compliance officer, any compensation they propose to receive for services that is in addition to the compensation or benefits received from their employer, including performance incentives offered by clients. Routing the disclosure through the supervisor or compliance officer puts it before the people who can evaluate the conflict and decide whether the arrangement may proceed.
rationales.B: No materiality floor applies. Any compensation the member proposes to receive for services in addition to the compensation or benefits received from the employer must be disclosed, including performance incentives offered by clients, whether or not the amount is large relative to base salary.
rationales.C: Telling a colleague does not discharge the duty. The disclosure must be made to the employer through the member's supervisor or compliance officer, because the point is to put the proposed arrangement before someone with the authority and responsibility to assess the conflict it creates.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), the content of a member's disclosure of additional compensation is most likely:

options.A: the monetary amount, and not its nature or duration.
options.B: the bare existence of the arrangement.
options.C: the nature, approximate amount, and duration.

rationales.A: Amount alone is not enough. The disclosure should include the terms of any agreement under which a member or candidate will receive additional compensation, and the nature of the compensation and the duration of the agreement are part of those terms. The employer needs both in order to judge how long the conflict will persist and what behaviour the arrangement rewards.
rationales.B: A bare statement that outside compensation exists does not satisfy the obligation. The disclosure should convey the terms of the agreement: the nature of the compensation, its approximate amount, and the duration of the agreement.
rationales.C: The disclosure should include the terms of any agreement under which a member or candidate will receive additional compensation, including the nature of the compensation, the approximate amount of compensation, and the duration of the agreement. Together these let the employer assess what the arrangement pays for, how large the incentive is, and how long it will shape the member's incentives.

questions.stem: Sound compliance practice for an additional-compensation arrangement under Standard IV(B) is most likely to:

options.A: treat the disclosed terms as confidential within the firm.
options.B: leave documentation of the arrangement to the employer.
options.C: have the paying party confirm the disclosed details.

rationales.A: Confidentiality from the paying party defeats the purpose of the disclosure. The party offering the additional compensation should acknowledge and confirm the details in the disclosure, which it cannot do if the terms are withheld from it.
rationales.B: Documentation by the employer alone is not the practice described. The party offering the additional compensation should acknowledge and confirm the details in the disclosure; the employer receives and evaluates it, but the independent confirmation comes from the offering party.
rationales.C: The party offering the additional compensation should acknowledge and confirm the details in the disclosure. Independent confirmation from that party strengthens the disclosure and enables the employer to verify the terms rather than rely solely on the member's account of the arrangement.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), nonmonetary compensation received for serving on the board of a company a member covers is most likely:

options.A: disclosable to the employer even without cash.
options.B: outside the reach of Standard IV(B).
options.C: free of any conflict requiring disclosure.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must disclose to their employer benefits received in exchange for their services, even where no cash is exchanged. Nonmonetary compensation may create a conflict of interest in the same manner as being paid to serve as a director: board service gives the member a personal incentive to recommend that company's stock, which can compromise loyalty to the employer and objectivity in making recommendations. The obligation is triggered by any benefit that may compromise that loyalty or objectivity, so the arrangement must be disclosed to the employer and consent obtained before the service is undertaken.
rationales.B: Standard IV(B) itself reaches compensation and benefits received from board service, so the matter is squarely within its scope rather than outside it. Standard VI(A) on disclosure of conflicts may apply in parallel to the same facts, but it applies alongside the duty owed to the employer, not instead of it.
rationales.C: The absence of cash does not remove the conflict. Nonmonetary benefits from a directorship — equity, options, services, perquisites, access — can compromise loyalty to the employer exactly as cash would, and the directorship itself creates a personal incentive to favor that company's securities. Disclosure to the employer is therefore still required.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(B), the most appropriate course for a member invited to an issuer-sponsored meeting is to:

options.A: report the trip afterward rather than seek approval.
options.B: decline all such invitations.
options.C: seek the employer's approval beforehand.

rationales.A: Reporting after the fact is not a substitute for approval beforehand. The sequence the guidance illustrates is approval from the employer before the meeting is accepted, refusal of lavish travel arrangements, and then disclosure of any hospitality received on return. Attending first and reporting later leaves the employer unable to judge the conflict until the member is already committed.
rationales.B: Issuer meetings are a legitimate part of research and need not be refused. The safeguards are procedural rather than abstentionist: obtain the employer's approval beforehand, decline lavish travel or other benefits that could compromise objectivity, and disclose the hospitality that is accepted. A blanket refusal is not what the standard asks for.
rationales.C: By gaining approval before accepting the meeting and declining the offered travel arrangements, the member avoids any potential conflict of interest between the employer and the issuer. Disclosing the hospitality received — a dinner, for instance — upon return then enables the firm to assess whether it has any impact on future reports and recommendations the member makes about that issuer. Where all of those steps are taken, Standard IV(B) is not violated.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), with respect to an employer's code of ethics, a member is most likely:

options.A: excused from recommending one where compliance procedures are detailed.
options.B: encouraged to recommend that the employer adopt one.
options.C: required to draft the code personally.

rationales.A: A code of ethics is not made redundant by detailed compliance procedures, because the two do different work. A code consists of fundamental, principle-based ethical concepts that apply to all of a firm's employees and conveys to employees and clients the ethical ideals investment professionals strive to achieve; compliance policies and procedures are the detailed means by which supervisors implement those concepts. The recommendation therefore stands whatever procedures a firm already maintains.
rationales.B: Members and candidates are encouraged to recommend that their employers adopt a code of ethics. Adoption of a code of ethics is critical to establishing a strong ethical foundation for investment advisory firms and their employees. Codes of ethics formally emphasize and reinforce the client loyalty responsibilities of investment firm personnel, protect investing clients by deterring misconduct, and protect the firm's reputation for integrity.
rationales.C: The encouragement is to recommend adoption, not to author the document. Drafting the code and implementing it through firm-wide procedures is the employer's responsibility; nothing in the standard makes a member personally responsible for writing the employer's code of ethics.

questions.stem: The relationship between a firm's code of ethics and its compliance policies and procedures is best characterized as:

options.A: distinct in purpose but complementary.
options.B: complementary but largely interchangeable.
options.C: best combined in a single document.

rationales.A: There is a distinction between codes of ethics and the specific policies and procedures needed to ensure compliance with the codes and with securities laws and regulations. Although both are important, codes of ethics should consist of fundamental, principle-based ethical concepts that apply to all of the firm's employees; in this way, firms can effectively convey to employees and clients the ethical ideals that investment professionals strive to achieve. Supervisors implement those concepts through detailed, firm-wide compliance policies and procedures. Standalone codes of ethics should be written in plain language and should address general ethical concepts, unencumbered by numerous detailed procedures or boilerplate legal terminology.
rationales.B: Neither substitutes for the other, so they are not interchangeable: the code states the principles and the procedures operationalize compliance with those principles and with securities laws and regulations. Both are important, and a firm that keeps only one of them has either ideals it cannot implement or mechanics with no stated purpose.
rationales.C: Folding every detailed procedure into the code buries the principles in mechanics. A standalone code should be written in plain language and address general ethical concepts, unencumbered by numerous detailed procedures or boilerplate legal terminology, precisely so that employees and clients can read what the firm stands for; the detailed procedures that implement it belong in a separate, firm-wide resource maintained by supervisors.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), a firm's code of ethics is most likely to be:

options.A: provided to clients as a matter of course.
options.B: kept internal to employees.
options.C: released only on written request.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should encourage their employers to provide their codes of ethics to clients. A simple, straightforward code of ethics, unencumbered by compliance procedures, will be effective in conveying that the firm is committed to conducting business in an ethical manner and in the best interests of the clients. That is why the code is kept short and principle-based: it is a document a client can actually read.
rationales.B: Keeping the code inside the firm forfeits its external value. Members should encourage employers to provide the code to clients, because doing so conveys the firm's commitment to conducting business ethically and in clients' best interests — a message that reaches no client if the document never leaves the staff handbook.
rationales.C: The guidance encourages providing the code to clients, not rationing it to those who think to ask in writing. A code supplied only on demand does little to convey the firm's commitment to acting ethically and in the best interests of clients, since most clients will never make the request.

questions.stem: Adequate compliance procedures under Standard IV(C) are best characterized as:

options.A: tailored to the firm's own operations.
options.B: copied from an industry template.
options.C: broad enough to anticipate every violation.

rationales.A: Adequate compliance procedures should be contained in a clearly written and accessible resource that is tailored to the firm's operations, and drafted so that the procedures are easy to understand. They should also designate a compliance officer whose authority and responsibility are clearly defined and who has the necessary resources and authority to implement the firm's compliance procedures and investigate potential legal and ethical violations; describe the hierarchy of supervision and assign duties among supervisors; implement a system of checks and balances; describe the scope of the procedures; include procedures to document the monitoring and testing of compliance procedures; detail permissible conduct; and delineate procedures for reporting violations and sanctions.
rationales.B: A template taken from an industry association is by definition not tailored to the firm's own operations, which is the first characteristic adequate procedures must have. Firms differ in the businesses they conduct, the conflicts those businesses create, and the supervisory hierarchy that has to police them, so the resource must be written for the firm it governs and must assign duties among that firm's actual supervisors.
rationales.C: Adequacy is not omniscience. The benchmark is a clearly written, accessible resource tailored to the firm and easy to understand, with a designated compliance officer, a described hierarchy of supervision, a system of checks and balances, a stated scope, documented monitoring and testing, detail on permissible conduct, and procedures for reporting violations and sanctions — not a document that foresees every violation that might ever occur.

questions.stem: Once a compliance program is in place, a supervisor is most likely to:

options.A: treat the oversight obligation as complete.
options.B: restrict it to senior management.
options.C: disseminate it to appropriate personnel.

rationales.A: Putting the program in place is the beginning of the obligation, not the end of it. The supervisor should seek to periodically update the program to ensure that the compliance measures are relevant, effective, and legally adequate; continually educate personnel regarding the compliance procedures; issue periodic compliance reminders; incorporate a professional conduct evaluation as part of an employee's performance review; monitor and review the actions of employees to ensure compliance and identify violators; and take the necessary steps to enforce the procedures once a violation has occurred.
rationales.B: Confining the program to senior management defeats its purpose. Its contents should be disseminated to appropriate personnel — the people whose conduct the procedures actually govern — and then reinforced through continual education, periodic compliance reminders, and a professional conduct evaluation within the performance review.
rationales.C: Once a compliance program is in place, a supervisor should disseminate the contents of the program to appropriate personnel; seek to periodically update the program to ensure that the compliance measures are relevant, effective, and legally adequate; continually educate personnel regarding the compliance procedures; issue periodic compliance reminders to appropriate personnel; incorporate a professional conduct evaluation as part of an employee's performance review; monitor and review the actions of employees to ensure compliance and identify violators; and take the necessary steps to enforce the procedures once a violation has occurred.

questions.stem: On discovering a violation, a supervisor is most likely required to:

options.A: wait for the next scheduled review.
options.B: rely on the employee's assurance.
options.C: respond to it promptly.

rationales.A: Waiting for a scheduled review is the failure itself. On discovery the supervisor should respond promptly, ensure a thorough investigation of the activities is conducted to determine the scope of the wrongdoing, increase supervision or place appropriate limitations on the alleged offender pending the outcome of the investigation, and review procedures for potential changes necessary to prevent future violations. Delay lets the conduct continue and the evidence of it decay.
rationales.B: An assurance from the person under suspicion is not a response. The supervisor must ensure a thorough investigation is conducted to determine the scope of the wrongdoing and, in the meantime, increase supervision of the alleged offender or place appropriate limitations on that person's activities pending the outcome — and then review the procedures that allowed the violation to happen.
rationales.C: Once a violation is discovered, a supervisor should respond promptly; ensure a thorough investigation of the activities is conducted to determine the scope of the wrongdoing; increase supervision or place appropriate limitations on the alleged offender pending the outcome of the investigation; and review procedures for potential changes necessary to prevent future violations from occurring.

questions.stem: Ethics and compliance training under Standard IV(C) is most likely:

options.A: regular and ongoing.
options.B: complete after onboarding.
options.C: redundant once a code is adopted.

rationales.A: Regular ethics and compliance training, in conjunction with adoption of a code of ethics, is critical to employers seeking to establish a strong culture of integrity and to provide an environment in which employees routinely engage in ethical conduct and comply with the law. Training and education assist individuals in both recognizing areas that are prone to ethical and legal pitfalls and identifying those circumstances and influences that can impair ethical judgment. By implementing education programs, supervisors can train their subordinates to put into practice what the firm's code of ethics requires.
rationales.B: One session at hire is not what the guidance contemplates: the training is to be regular. The circumstances and influences that impair ethical judgment change as an employee's role and the firm's business change, and it is periodic reinforcement that keeps the code in practice rather than on file.
rationales.C: Training is not made redundant by the code; it operates in conjunction with it. Adopting the document communicates the firm's ethical ideals, but education is how supervisors train subordinates to put into practice what the code requires, and how employees learn to recognize the areas prone to ethical and legal pitfalls and the influences that can impair their judgment.

questions.stem: With respect to the firm's incentive structure, Standard IV(C) most likely requires supervisors to:

options.A: ask whether revenue targets are ambitious enough.
options.B: leave the ethics of compensation to the board.
options.C: ask whether rewards undercut ethical conduct.

rationales.A: The question is not whether the targets are demanding but whether the structure encourages profits and returns at the expense of ethically appropriate conduct. Problematic reward structures may take no account of how desired outcomes are achieved, and in doing so encourage dysfunctional or counterproductive behavior; a more ambitious target sharpens that pressure rather than relieving it.
rationales.B: The incentive structure sits squarely within the compliance practices expected of supervisors and firms, who must look closely at it because it is what shapes conduct day to day. Deferring the whole question to the board leaves the firm's most powerful driver of behavior unexamined by the people who supervise that behavior.
rationales.C: Supervisors and firms must look closely at their incentive structure to determine whether the structure encourages profits and returns at the expense of ethically appropriate conduct. Problematic reward structures may not take into account how desired outcomes are achieved and encourage dysfunctional or counterproductive behavior. Employees will work to achieve a culture of integrity when compensation and incentives are tied to how outcomes are achieved rather than how much revenue is generated for the firm.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), the compliance tools available to a supervisor with limited authority are most likely:

options.A: the firm's electronic trade surveillance systems.
options.B: unavailable where the firm withholds compliance resources.
options.C: built with the supervisor's own superiors in the firm.

rationales.A: Standard IV(C) contemplates a broad toolkit rather than a single technology. The guidance names a code of ethics, compliance policies and procedures, education and training programs, an incentive structure that rewards ethical conduct, and adoption of firm-wide best practice standards such as the GIPS standards and the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct. Electronic trade surveillance can serve the monitoring and enforcement part of that structure, but a supervisor who buys surveillance software and stops there has left the preventive elements of the system unbuilt.
rationales.B: Limited authority, or a firm that declines to fund compliance, does not leave the supervisor without tools and does not extinguish the supervisory obligation. The guidance is explicit that such limitations should not prevent members and candidates from working with their own superiors and within the firm structure to develop and implement effective compliance tools. The supervisor therefore still has avenues: raise the deficiency with superiors, build what can be built within the existing structure, and, where the firm will not establish a reasonable compliance system, decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until adequate procedures are adopted.
rationales.C: Standard IV(C) guidance states that limitations on a supervisor's authority should not prevent members and candidates from working with their own superiors and within the firm structure to develop and implement effective compliance tools, including but not limited to: (1) a code of ethics; (2) compliance policies and procedures; (3) education and training programs; (4) an incentive structure that rewards ethical conduct; and (5) adoption of firm-wide best practice standards, for example the GIPS standards and the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct. The tools are thus developed through the firm's own hierarchy and in cooperation with the supervisor's superiors, which is why they are neither foreclosed by thin authority nor reducible to surveillance technology.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), a supervisor's duty to supervise is most likely satisfied by:

options.A: assuming the system is adequate and awaiting a regulator's view.
options.B: knowing what an adequate system requires and enforcing it.
options.C: leaving the firm's compliance architecture to the compliance staff.

rationales.A: Assuming the existing system is adequate and waiting for a regulator to identify a deficiency is the opposite of the reasonable effort the standard demands. The duty is anticipatory: the supervisor must know what an adequate system looks like for this firm and act to put one in place, then monitor and enforce it. A regulatory finding is evidence that the duty was already breached, not the trigger that creates it.
rationales.B: Members and candidates with supervisory responsibility must understand what constitutes an adequate compliance system for their firms and make reasonable efforts to see that appropriate compliance procedures are established, documented, communicated to covered personnel, and followed. Adequate procedures are those designed to meet industry standards, regulatory requirements, the requirements of the Code and Standards, and the circumstances of the firm. Once compliance procedures are established, the supervisor must also make reasonable efforts to ensure that the procedures are monitored and enforced, so the duty runs from design through communication to ongoing enforcement.
rationales.C: The supervisor may rely on a compliance department to draft and administer procedures, but the understanding itself cannot be delegated away. The standard places the obligation to know what an adequate system comprises, and to make reasonable efforts to see that procedures are established, documented, communicated to covered personnel, followed, monitored and enforced, on the member or candidate with supervisory responsibility.

questions.stem: When supervision is delegated to a subordinate, Standard IV(C) most likely requires the supervisor to:

options.A: instruct the delegate in methods that promote compliance.
options.B: leave compliance judgments to the delegate's discretion.
options.C: rely on the delegate's prior supervisory experience.

rationales.A: A member's or candidate's responsibilities under Standard IV(C) include instructing those subordinates to whom supervision is delegated about methods to promote compliance, including preventing and detecting violations of laws, rules, regulations, firm policies, and the Code and Standards. Delegation moves the task, not the duty: the delegating supervisor retains ultimate responsibility for the conduct of those supervised, which is why the instruction must be given at the point of delegation rather than assumed.
rationales.B: Leaving compliance judgments to the delegate's discretion does not sever the chain of responsibility. The supervisor must instruct the delegate on methods to promote compliance and to prevent and detect violations, and must then make reasonable efforts to see that the delegated supervision is actually carried out, because ultimate responsibility for the supervised employees remains with the delegating supervisor.
rationales.C: Experience gained under another firm's policies is not a substitute for instruction in this firm's compliance methods, policies and reporting expectations. The standard requires the supervisor to instruct the delegate about methods to promote compliance, including preventing and detecting violations of laws, rules, regulations, firm policies, and the Code and Standards, without an exemption for seasoned delegates.

questions.stem: On learning that an employee may have violated the law, a supervisor under Standard IV(C) is most likely required to:

options.A: promptly assess how far the wrongdoing extends.
options.B: rely on the employee's account of the conduct.
options.C: raise the matter at the next compliance audit.

rationales.A: Once a supervisor learns that an employee has violated or may have violated the law or engaged in unethical behavior, the supervisor must promptly initiate an assessment to determine the extent of the wrongdoing. Relying on the employee's statements about the extent of the violation, or on assurances that the wrongdoing will not reoccur, is not enough; reporting the misconduct to the appropriate compliance and management personnel and warning the employee to cease the activity are also not enough. Pending the outcome of the investigation, the supervisor must take steps to ensure the violation will not be repeated, such as placing limits on the employee's activities or increasing the monitoring of those activities.
rationales.B: The guidance specifically rejects reliance on the wrongdoer's own account. Statements about the extent of the violation and assurances that it will not recur do not discharge the duty, because the person with the strongest incentive to understate the problem is being asked to define its scope. The supervisor must instead initiate an assessment of the extent of the wrongdoing and impose interim controls while it proceeds.
rationales.C: The required response is prompt. Waiting for the next audit cycle leaves the employee in place with unchanged authority and allows the conduct to continue or to be concealed. Pending the outcome of the assessment the supervisor must act at once to prevent repetition, for example by limiting the employee's activities or increasing monitoring of them.

questions.stem: The compliance practices of Standard IV(C) most likely advise a supervisor to:

options.A: review conduct apart from the employee's performance review.
options.B: review conduct once a violation has been reported.
options.C: review conduct within the employee's performance review.

rationales.A: Holding ethics apart from the formal review signals that conduct is a peripheral concern rather than a performance factor. The recommended practice runs the other way: the professional conduct evaluation belongs inside the performance review, alongside the production and revenue measures that otherwise dominate it.
rationales.B: A purely reactive evaluation arrives too late to deter anything. The recommended practice treats professional conduct as a standing item in every employee's performance review, so that ethical behaviour is measured and rewarded routinely rather than examined only once a violation has surfaced.
rationales.C: Standard IV(C) compliance practices recommend that supervisors incorporate a professional conduct evaluation as part of an employee's performance review. Doing so makes ethical conduct a measurable performance factor rather than a peripheral concern, and it complements the related recommendation to establish an incentive structure that does not reward results obtained by improper means.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), the effect of corporate culture on an individual's ethical conduct is most likely that:

options.A: an ethical culture can arise without senior management's example.
options.B: a culture of integrity can replace formal compliance procedures.
options.C: a results-at-any-cost culture can override good intentions.

rationales.A: Individual resolve is not sufficient protection. Even employees who want to make the right choices, and who recognise the obstacles to ethical conduct, can be pushed into improper behaviour by the culture around them. An ethical culture therefore does not arise on its own from the bottom up: the guidance assigns supervisors and senior management an active role in building and reinforcing a culture of integrity.
rationales.B: Culture and procedures are complements, not substitutes. A culture of integrity reinforces an individual's natural desire to act ethically, but Standard IV(C) still requires adequate compliance procedures that are established, documented, communicated to covered personnel, followed, monitored and enforced. Neither element discharges the duty on its own.
rationales.C: Standard IV(C) guidance on establishing an appropriate incentive structure states that even if individuals want to make the right choices and follow an ethical course of conduct, and are aware of the obstacles that impair ethical conduct, they can still be influenced to act improperly by a corporate culture that embraces a 'succeed at all costs' mentality, stresses results regardless of the methods used to achieve those results, and does not reward ethical behavior. Supervisors can reinforce an individual's natural desire to act ethically by building a culture of integrity in the workplace, which is why the incentive structure is treated as a supervisory responsibility.

questions.stem: Under Standard IV(C), the conduct that constitutes reasonable supervision is most likely:

options.A: set by the number of compliance staff the firm employs.
options.B: set by the number and the work of those supervised.
options.C: set by one benchmark applying to every supervisor and firm.

rationales.A: The number of compliance personnel employed is an input to the system, not the measure of whether supervision was reasonable. A large compliance department attached to procedures that are undocumented, uncommunicated or unenforced does not satisfy the standard, while a small team with procedures matched to the activity being supervised may. The test looks to the employees supervised and the work they perform.
rationales.B: The conduct that constitutes reasonable supervision in a particular case depends on the number of employees supervised and the work performed by those employees. The supervisor's obligations therefore scale with organizational context: a small team may permit personal review of each employee's conduct, whereas larger teams require delegated supervisory structures, written procedures and systemic controls to achieve the same reasonable effort.
rationales.C: There is no single benchmark of supervisory conduct that applies across firms. What is reasonable depends on how many employees are supervised and on the nature of the work they perform, so the same procedures that are adequate for a two-person team can fall well short for a large trading desk carrying out complex, high-risk activity.
